passage: I'm Jahnavi. Last summer, when Nirmala Mausi's blue cup broke, she asked me if I'd touched it. I hadn't. But my eyes started blinking fast, blink-blink-blink, and I couldn't stop them. “See, your eyes are telling me,” she said. My throat closed up. I had been reading on the tablet for two hours, so my eyes were already dry and stinging, and then I was scared on top of that. Later the cat was found on the shelf, next to the pieces. Mausi hugged me and said, “Blinking isn't a lie detector. I'm sorry.” I still blink when I'm nervous. Now I know that's all it means.

qa.q: Where was the cat found?
qa.a: The cat was found on the shelf, next to the pieces.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling while blinking fast?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt scared of being blamed, on top of eyes already dry from two hours on the tablet, so the blinking came from nerves and tiredness, not guilt.

qa.q: What went wrong in Mausi's first reading, and what fixed it?
qa.a: She treated blinking as proof of lying; finding the cat, saying sorry and accepting that blinking isn't a lie detector fixed it.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Mausi feel after the cat was found?
qa.a: She probably felt guilty and sorry for doubting Jahnavi only because of blinking.

grounding: Shows a child's nervous, screen-tired blinking being mistaken for lying, and the adult learning it is not evidence of dishonesty.

passage: Reading-group note, Thursday. Nikita, Class 3 teacher. Chaitanya blinked constantly while reading aloud today, sometimes six or seven blinks on one line. Mr Rao, who covered my class on Monday, wrote that Chaitanya “doesn't focus and seems shifty.” I don't agree. When he reads to me alone, the blinking nearly stops. In front of the group it starts again, and his voice speeds up. He also told me his eyes feel scratchy after screen time at home. For now he will read to a partner, and I've asked his parents to get his eyes checked if the scratchiness keeps going.

qa.q: When does Chaitanya's blinking nearly stop?
qa.a: The blinking nearly stops when he reads to Nikita alone.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's blinking in front of the group most likely show?
qa.a: It most likely shows he feels nervous reading to an audience, with scratchy eyes after screen time adding to it, rather than a lack of focus.

qa.q: What two steps did Nikita take, and why do they fit?
qa.a: Nikita let him read to a partner to ease the nerves and asked his parents to get his eyes checked if the scratchiness keeps going, covering both likely causes.

qa.q: Why might Mr Rao read the blinking differently?
qa.a: Mr Rao saw Chaitanya only briefly and may believe blinking means shifty or unfocused, without seeing him read calmly alone.

grounding: Shows a child's frequent blinking while reading aloud being read as shiftiness, when nerves and dry eyes explain it better.

passage: Tuesday night. Dear diary, it's me, Nazia. Today at lunch I told Ankita I'd finished the whole mystery book. She squinted at me. “You're blinking loads. You're lying.” I WASN'T. My eyes have been itchy since swimming yesterday, and then she stared, and I got nervous, and they blinked even more. I said, “Ask me the ending, then.” I told her the ending. She went quiet and said, “Okay, sorry, my cousin says blinking means lying.” I said her cousin should get itchy eyes one day. We laughed. But it felt bad for a minute, being called a liar because of my eyelids 😔

qa.q: Why had Nazia's eyes been itchy?
qa.a: Nazia's eyes had been itchy since swimming yesterday.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Ankita called the blinking lying?
qa.a: Nazia felt nervous and hurt at being called a liar, and the nerves made the itchy eyes blink even more.

qa.q: What worked in how Nazia answered?
qa.a: Offering to tell the ending gave real evidence instead of arguing about blinking, and it cleared things up calmly.

qa.q: Where did Ankita's idea come from, and how might she feel now?
qa.a: Ankita got it from her cousin, and after hearing the ending she probably felt a bit embarrassed for the accusation.

grounding: Shows a child's nervous blinking, worsened by itchy eyes, being mistaken for lying by a friend, and evidence clearing it up.

passage: Ten minutes before the exam, Chetan handed Neelam's pen back across the aisle. She narrowed her eyes at him, hard, lips tight. His stomach flipped. Did I break it? Is she angry I kept it all week? He almost moved seats. Then the sun slid behind the building across the road, and the glare blazing off the blackboard went dull. Neelam's face relaxed. She rubbed her eyes and grinned at him. “Thanks. I forgot my glasses, and that board was killing me.” Chetan let out his breath and looked where she had been looking. The board was still hard to read.

qa.q: What had Neelam forgotten?
qa.a: Neelam had forgotten her glasses.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when Neelam narrowed her eyes?
qa.a: He felt anxious and a little guilty, worried he'd broken her pen or kept it too long and that she was angry.

qa.q: What could Chetan try next time a look worries him?
qa.a: He could check the context, such as glare or light, or simply ask, before deciding the look is about him.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Neelam?
qa.a: Neelam was struggling to read the board in the glare without her glasses and wasn't thinking about the pen at all.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's narrowed eyes as anger, when glare and missing glasses explain the squint.

passage: At the evening tuition centre in Hyderabad, Varun announced he had solved the puzzle on the whiteboard first. From the back row, Yusuf narrowed his eyes at him. Varun's face went hot. He thinks I copied. He'd been caught once last term, and he felt every eye on him. At the break he walked over, ready to argue. Then he saw Yusuf leaning close to his own notebook, nose almost on the page. “Why were you giving me that look?” “What look? I can't read the board from back there. It's all blurry.” Varun sat down beside him. “Tell your ammi. My brother got glasses for that.”

qa.q: Where was Yusuf sitting?
qa.a: Yusuf was sitting in the back row.

qa.q: Why did Varun's face go hot when Yusuf narrowed his eyes?
qa.a: Varun felt embarrassed and defensive, fearing Yusuf thought he had copied, especially since he'd been caught once before.

qa.q: What helped Varun avoid an unfair argument?
qa.a: He noticed Yusuf leaning close to his notebook and asked about the look, which showed the real reason was blurry vision.

qa.q: What might Yusuf's evenings at tuition be like?
qa.a: Yusuf probably struggles to follow the board and may feel frustrated, without realising his squint looks like suspicion.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's narrowed eyes as suspicion, and checking the context to find a vision problem instead.

passage: “Why are you glaring at me?” Shalini stopped with the relay baton in her hand. Devika, standing at the edge of the track, had her eyes screwed up to slits. “I'm not glaring.” “You are. Since I dropped the baton, you've been giving me that look.” “Shalini, the sun is right behind you. I can't see your face at all. You're just a black shape.” Shalini turned. The sun was blazing over the pavilion, straight into Devika's eyes. “Oh.” “Come stand here.” Shalini did. Devika's face opened up. “See? Now I can see you. And the drop wasn't your fault. The hand-off was bad.”

qa.q: Where was the sun?
qa.a: The sun was blazing over the pavilion, straight into Devika's eyes.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she asked about the glaring?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed after dropping the baton, and read Devika's narrowed eyes as blame.

qa.q: What did Shalini do that cleared things up?
qa.a: She asked directly and then turned to check the light, which showed the squint came from the sun.

qa.q: How did Devika see the whole exchange?
qa.a: Devika couldn't even see Shalini's face against the sun, so she was surprised to be accused and quick to reassure her 🙂

grounding: Shows a child reading a teammate's squint as anger, and checking the light to find the real cause.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: Diary, Friday. Avni here. Reena Ma'am called my name in assembly today because my poem won. Everyone turned round. I couldn't look up. I stared at the shoelace of the girl in front and felt my ears burn. After, Pooja said, “You didn't even look at Ma'am. That's so rude.” I wasn't being rude! I was so happy and so shy that my eyes wouldn't go up. At home I told Nani, and she said, “In my village we lowered our eyes to teachers anyway. It was respect.” Maybe next time I'll look up for one second and then down again.

qa.q: Why did Reena Ma'am call Avni's name?
qa.a: She called Avni's name because Avni's poem won.

qa.q: Why couldn't Avni look up in assembly?
qa.a: Avni felt happy but very shy with everyone turning round, so the lowered eyes came from shyness, not rudeness.

qa.q: What small step does Avni plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: Looking up for one second and then down lets Avni show thanks to Reena Ma'am without feeling overwhelmed.

qa.q: How did Pooja read Avni's lowered eyes?
qa.a: Pooja saw rudeness, not knowing Avni was shy and that, as Nani said, lowered eyes can show respect.

grounding: Shows a child looking away when praised in public out of shyness, not defiance, and lowered eyes to elders as a sign of respect.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: Disha had three raw mangoes in her frock pocket when Lalit Chacha came round the side of the cowshed. “Whose tree are those from?” Disha stared at the dust by her feet. She said nothing. “Look at me when I'm speaking!” Her chin sank lower, and her toes curled. Dadi, shelling peanuts on the charpai, spoke up. “Lalit, she's not being stubborn. Look how red her ears are. She's ashamed.” Lalit crouched so he wasn't towering. “Disha. Were they from the Patil tree?” A tiny nod. “Then we'll take them back together, and you'll say sorry.” Disha looked up, just for a second.

qa.q: How many mangoes did Disha have?
qa.a: Disha had three raw mangoes in her frock pocket.

qa.q: What did Disha's lowered eyes and curled toes show?
qa.a: They showed she felt ashamed at being caught, not defiant, as Dadi pointed out from her red ears.

qa.q: What changed when Lalit crouched down?
qa.a: By lowering himself and asking a simple question, he made it easier for Disha to answer and to agree to return the mangoes.

qa.q: Why might Lalit have read Disha's silence as stubbornness?
qa.a: Not meeting his eyes looked to him like refusing to listen, so at first he missed the shame behind it.

grounding: Shows a child looking away when caught out, a sign of shame rather than defiance, and an elder helping an adult read it.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: In the Helsinki classroom, Liam read his answer aloud: “Twelve.” Ms Ulla Virtanen shook her head gently. “Not quite. Look again at the second line.” Liam's eyes slid away to the window, to the snow on the bike racks. He didn't look back. A classmate muttered, “He's ignoring her.” Ms Virtanen watched his face: pink, jaw tight, eyes blinking at the glass. She walked over and crouched by his desk, looking at his workbook rather than at him. “It's just the carry. Here.” Liam's eyes came back to the page. “Oh. Fourteen,” he whispered.

qa.q: What answer did Liam first read aloud?
qa.a: Liam first read aloud the answer twelve.

qa.q: What does Liam looking at the window suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt embarrassed at being corrected in front of the class, not that he was ignoring the teacher.

qa.q: How did Ms Virtanen help Liam come back to the task?
qa.a: She crouched beside him and looked at the workbook rather than his face, which took away the pressure and let him try again.

qa.q: How did the classmate who muttered read Liam's look?
qa.a: The classmate took it as ignoring the teacher, missing the pink face and tight jaw that showed embarrassment.

grounding: Shows a child averting the gaze when corrected in class out of embarrassment, not defiance, and a teacher easing the pressure.

subtype: Eye contact norms with elders in India [Mismatch]
passage: Counsellor's note, Tuesday. Seema, school counsellor. Vikas joined us from a small-town school in July. His homeroom teacher, new from Canada, flagged him: “Won't meet my eyes when I ask about missing homework. Possibly not being truthful.” I met Vikas today. He sat very straight, hands folded, eyes lowered, and called me Ma'am in every sentence. When I asked why he looks down, he looked puzzled. “At home, staring at an elder who is scolding you is badtameezi.” His homework was missing because his family's power has been cut for a week. I've shared all this with his teacher, and we'll explain both customs to Vikas.

qa.q: Why was Vikas's homework missing?
qa.a: His homework was missing because his family's power has been cut for a week.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when asked why he looks down?
qa.a: He felt puzzled, since at home lowered eyes show respect, and he was probably anxious about the missing homework too.

qa.q: What did Seema do that helped both Vikas and his teacher?
qa.a: She asked Vikas directly, found the real reason for the homework and shared the cultural meaning with his teacher.

qa.q: How did the homeroom teacher first read Vikas's lowered eyes?
qa.a: The teacher read them as possibly not truthful, because where the teacher comes from, steady eye contact signals honesty.

grounding: Shows a child's lowered eyes toward elders, taught as respect at home, being misread as dishonesty under a different school norm.

subtype: Eye contact norms with elders in India [Mismatch]
passage: Wednesday. Zainab's diary. Mrs Binita Shah stopped me after class at my new school in Leicester. She said, kindly, “Here we look at people when they talk to us, love. Otherwise they might think you're hiding something.” I nearly cried. At home in Lucknow, Abbu always said lowering your eyes to a teacher is adab, good manners. I told her that. She smiled and said her Nani taught her the same thing in Gujarat. “You're not wrong. It's just different here. Maybe look at my eyebrows? That's a nice middle.” I tried it in maths. It felt strange, but not rude.

qa.q: Where did Mrs Binita Shah's Nani teach her the same thing?
qa.a: Her Nani taught her the same thing in Gujarat.

qa.q: Why did Zainab nearly cry after class?
qa.a: Zainab felt hurt and confused, having been taught at home that lowered eyes are good manners and now hearing it might look like hiding something.

qa.q: What middle way did Mrs Shah suggest?
qa.a: She suggested looking at her eyebrows, which lets Zainab meet the school's expectation without feeling rude.

qa.q: How does Mrs Shah understand both sides?
qa.a: She grew up with the same custom from her Nani, so she knows lowered eyes can be respect even though her school expects eye contact.

grounding: Shows a child's lowered eyes with elders meeting a school norm of steady eye contact, with neither being proof of honesty or disrespect.

subtype: Eye contact norms with elders in India [Mismatch]
passage: The inspector from the city, Usha Madam, came to the hill school in Kullu on a cold morning. She stopped by Tenzin's bench. “Did you write this essay yourself?” Tenzin stood up, hands behind his back, eyes on her shoes. “Yes, Madam.” “Then why won't you look at me?” His eyes stayed down, his ears reddening. The village teacher said quietly, “Madam, here the children are taught not to stare at elders. It's how they show respect.” Usha paused. She asked Tenzin to tell her what the essay was about. He told her, eyes still lowered, every detail of the yak fair. She nodded. “Your own words, clearly.”

qa.q: What was Tenzin's essay about?
qa.a: Tenzin's essay was about the yak fair.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when Usha asked why he wouldn't look at her?
qa.a: He probably felt nervous and embarrassed, trying to show respect the way he was taught, not hiding anything.

qa.q: What did Usha do that was fairer than judging his eyes?
qa.a: She asked Tenzin to explain the essay, using what he knew as evidence instead of his gaze.

qa.q: How might the village teacher see the inspector's question?
qa.a: The teacher might worry that a respectful child was being misjudged and so stepped in to explain the custom.

grounding: Shows a child's lowered eyes with an elder signalling respect, misread at first as hiding something, and neither being proof of honesty.

passage: Damini, you think your papa never rolled his eyes? Let me, your old Dada Madhav, tell you. When he was nine, I asked him every evening to fetch the milk. One day he rolled his eyes so hard I thought they'd stick. I was about to shout. Then I remembered my own father shouting, and how I'd go silent and stew. So I sat down on the step and asked, “What's wrong with the milk?” He was quiet. Then it came out: the bigger boys teased him at the dairy. That same evening we walked there together, and after that he went with his cousin. The eye-rolling stopped soon after.

qa.q: What did Madhav ask his son to fetch every evening?
qa.a: He asked him to fetch the milk.

qa.q: What was the boy feeling behind his eye-roll?
qa.a: It looked like annoyance, but the boy was probably embarrassed and scared of the bigger boys who teased him at the dairy.

qa.q: What choice did Madhav make instead of shouting, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He sat down and calmly asked what was wrong, which let his son explain the teasing so they could fix the real problem.

qa.q: How might the boy have felt when his father walked with him to the dairy?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and protected, knowing his father had taken the teasing seriously.

grounding: Shows a child's eye-roll as a way to avoid a spoken argument, and a parent's calm question opening a better talk.

passage: The fan had stopped working, the last period was dragging, and the corridor outside was loud with another class's practice. Salma Ma'am asked Karthik to rewrite his paragraph neatly. Karthik rolled his eyes, slowly, all the way up to the ceiling. A few kids went “Ooooh.” Salma felt the heat rise in her own face. Instead of snapping, she walked over and spoke under the noise. “That eye-roll said something. What is it?” Karthik scowled at his notebook. “My hand hurts. I already wrote it twice. And it's so hot.” She looked at his cramped, sweaty writing. “Fair. Rewrite just the first three lines. Water first.”

qa.q: How many lines did Salma Ma'am ask Karthik to rewrite in the end?
qa.a: She asked him to rewrite just the first three lines.

qa.q: What was Karthik most likely feeling when he rolled his eyes?
qa.a: It most likely expressed frustration and tiredness, since his hand hurt, he'd written it twice and the room was hot, rather than pure disrespect.

qa.q: Why did asking about the eye-roll work better than snapping?
qa.a: Asking calmly under the noise let Karthik say what was wrong, so Salma could adjust the task instead of starting a power struggle.

qa.q: What was it like for Salma when the class went “Ooooh”?
qa.a: She felt her face heat up, as if her authority was being tested, which made staying calm harder.

grounding: Shows a teacher reading a child's eye-roll as annoyance, and calmly asking what was wrong to open a better talk.

passage: In their flat in Nagpur, Urmila was helping her younger sister Sonali pack her bag for the school trip. “Take the jacket. It gets cold on the bus.” Sonali rolled her eyes and zipped the bag shut. Urmila's first thought was, Fine, freeze then. She almost said it. Instead she sat on the bed. “You rolled your eyes. Is it the jacket, or me?” Sonali picked at the zip. “It's the jacket. It's the old pink one. Everyone will laugh.” “Ah.” Urmila went to her cupboard and held out her own grey hoodie. “Borrow this?” Sonali grinned and unzipped the bag.

qa.q: Where was Sonali going?
qa.a: Sonali was going on the school trip.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when Sonali rolled her eyes?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and brushed off, nearly snapping, before choosing to ask instead.

qa.q: What did asking reveal that the eye-roll hid?
qa.a: It showed Sonali was embarrassed about the old pink jacket, not rejecting her sister's advice, so the hoodie solved it.

qa.q: What was the jacket worry like for Sonali?
qa.a: Sonali was afraid others would laugh at the old pink jacket, and rolling her eyes was easier than saying so.

grounding: Shows an older sibling reading an eye-roll as dismissal, and a calm question revealing embarrassment underneath.

passage: Music room note, Saturday. Vidya, harmonium teacher. During today's practice exam Gurleen sucked her cheeks in and chewed the inside of one the whole time she played. From the side it looked like a sour face. The visiting examiner wrote “seems unhappy to be here, attitude?” on her sheet. I've taught Gurleen for two years. She does this whenever a piece gets hard, and also when she's nervous, like today. It's how she steadies herself. I spoke to the examiner and had the comment removed. I told Gurleen her face is her own business, but if her cheek gets sore, we can try slow breaths instead.

qa.q: What did the visiting examiner write on Gurleen's sheet?
qa.a: The examiner wrote “seems unhappy to be here, attitude?” on her sheet.

qa.q: What was Gurleen most likely feeling as she chewed her cheek?
qa.a: She was most likely nervous about the exam and concentrating hard on a difficult piece, not unhappy or rude.

qa.q: Which of Vidya's steps helped Gurleen most?
qa.a: Having the unfair comment removed protected Gurleen, and offering slow breaths for a sore cheek respected the habit while giving another option.

qa.q: Why might the examiner read the face as attitude?
qa.a: Seeing Gurleen only once and from the side, the examiner took the sucked-in cheeks for a sour face, without knowing her habit.

grounding: Shows a child's cheek-chewing from nerves and concentration being misread as attitude, and a teacher explaining it is a self-soothing habit.

passage: Sunday night. It's Indu, writing in bed. Today Leela showed me her drawing of our street for the competition. I was also thinking about my own entry, which I haven't finished, and I was chewing the inside of my cheek like I always do when I'm worried. Leela's face fell. “You hate it. You made a face.” I didn't even know my face was doing anything! I told her about the cheek thing and said the windows in her drawing are better than mine. She said, “Then stop chewing, you look like you ate a lemon.” I laughed, but I'll probably still do it. It helps me think.

qa.q: What was Leela's drawing of?
qa.a: Leela's drawing was of their street, for the competition.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling while chewing the inside of the cheek?
qa.a: Indu felt worried about the unfinished entry, and the chewing was a self-soothing habit, not a comment on Leela's drawing.

qa.q: How did Indu fix the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Indu explained the cheek-chewing habit and gave real praise for the windows, which reassured Leela.

qa.q: How did Leela see Indu's face?
qa.a: Leela saw a face of dislike and felt hurt, until Indu explained it.

grounding: Shows a child's nervous cheek-chewing being mistaken for a grimace of dislike, when it is a self-soothing habit.

passage: Outside the kirana shop in their small town, Naveen was fixing the slipped chain on his cycle, cheeks sucked in so hard his face looked hollow. Simran walked past with her mother's shopping bag and waved. Naveen didn't wave back; his cheeks stayed pinched, his jaw working. Simran's smile dropped. Still angry about the kho-kho game, then. She almost walked on. Then she noticed his oily fingers, the chain half-hooked, and his tongue pressing inside one cheek. She waited. The chain clicked in. Naveen's face relaxed completely. “Oh, Simran! Hi! Did you see? I fixed it myself.”

qa.q: What was Naveen fixing?
qa.a: Naveen was fixing the slipped chain on his cycle.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when Naveen didn't wave back?
qa.a: She felt hurt and uneasy, thinking he was still angry about the kho-kho game.

qa.q: What did Simran do that stopped a misunderstanding?
qa.a: She looked at the context, his oily fingers and the half-hooked chain, and waited instead of walking off.

qa.q: What was the moment like for Naveen?
qa.a: Naveen was so focused on the chain that he didn't notice Simran at first, and felt proud and happy once it clicked in.

grounding: Shows a child's drawn-in cheeks while concentrating looking like ill will, when it is a focus habit.

passage: Thursday. Sharmila's diary. At lunch I opened my tiffin, Ma's fish curry and rice, and Sarika wrinkled her nose. Right away my face went hot. Last year a girl called my lunch smelly, and I ate in the corridor for a week. I nearly closed the lid. But Sarika wasn't even looking at my box. I asked, trying to sound normal, “Is it my fish?” She said, “What? No! Someone's thrown a banana peel in the bin behind you. It stinks.” Then she asked if she could try a bite of the fish. She liked it! Tomorrow I'm bringing extra.

qa.q: What was in Sharmila's tiffin?
qa.a: Sharmila's tiffin had Ma's fish curry and rice.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila's face go hot when Sarika wrinkled her nose?
qa.a: Sharmila felt hurt and embarrassed, remembering being teased about lunch last year and fearing it was happening again.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking kindly, “Is it my fish?”, worked because it showed the smell came from the bin, not the lunch, and led to sharing 😊

qa.q: What did the wrinkled nose really mean for Sarika?
qa.a: Sarika was reacting to the stinking banana peel in the bin, and she was happy to try the fish.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's wrinkled nose as dislike of their lunch, and asking kindly to find another cause.

passage: Under the neem tree at the village school, Zeenat unwrapped her roti and her Nani's garlic pickle and held some out to Deepak. His nose wrinkled up, lips pulled back. Zeenat's hand stopped in the air. Her Nani had made it specially, and Zeenat had carried it all the way from the fields. She almost put it away without a word. Instead she asked, “You don't like garlic?” Deepak coughed. “I love garlic. It's the smoke. They're burning stubble past the canal, can't you smell it?” Zeenat sniffed. The air was sharp and grey. Deepak took the pickle, and his nose wrinkled again, at the smoke.

qa.q: Where were they burning stubble?
qa.a: They were burning stubble past the canal.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when her hand stopped in the air?
qa.a: Zeenat felt hurt and let down, thinking Deepak disliked the pickle her Nani had made specially.

qa.q: How did Zeenat avoid assuming rejection?
qa.a: She asked a simple question instead of silently putting the pickle away, which showed the smoke caused the wrinkled nose.

qa.q: What was the lunch break like for Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak was bothered by the sharp stubble smoke and coughing, and had no idea his face looked like dislike of the pickle.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's wrinkled nose as rejection of their food, and asking kindly to find the real cause.

passage: In Hiroshi's second week at the school in Nairobi, he unwrapped his onigiri at the lunch table. Wanjiru, beside him, wrinkled her nose and turned her face away. Hiroshi's shoulders came up. At his old school, a boy had pinched his nose at this same seaweed. He started folding the wrapper back over. Then he stopped and asked, very quietly, “Does it smell bad to you?” Wanjiru looked surprised. “Your rice? No! The wall behind us was painted this morning. My head is spinning from it.” She pointed at the shiny wall and the sign. They moved to the window table, and she asked what was inside.

qa.q: When had the wall behind them been painted?
qa.a: The wall behind them was painted that morning.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi's shoulders come up?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and wary, remembering a boy pinching his nose at the same seaweed at his old school.

qa.q: What went right when Hiroshi asked quietly?
qa.a: Asking brought out the real cause, the fresh paint, and turned a hurtful moment into a shared move and a new friendship.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru feel knowing her face made Hiroshi start to fold his lunch away?
qa.a: Wanjiru would probably feel sorry and glad he asked, since she meant nothing against his food.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's wrinkled nose as dislike of their lunch, and asking kindly to avoid assuming rejection.

subtype: Curling a lip and lip trembling in embarrassment [Mismatch]
passage: Monday: Usha won the class monitor vote by two votes. When the teacher pinned up the result, Nilesh's upper lip curled, and he muttered, “Teacher's pet.” The teacher saw, said nothing in front of everyone, and asked him to stay back at break. Wednesday: Two of Usha's friends sang “Two votes, two votes” at Nilesh in the line. His lower lip began to tremble. The teacher handed him the register. “Take this to the office for me, please.” Outside, the teacher asked what had been happening since Monday. Friday: Nilesh and Usha were paired for the quiz. He didn't curl his lip once. They won by two points.

qa.q: By how many votes did Usha win?
qa.a: Usha won the class monitor vote by two votes.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have been feeling when his lower lip trembled on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and humiliated by the singing and trying not to cry in front of the class; the earlier curl of scorn likely came from the same disappointment.

qa.q: How did the teacher protect Nilesh's dignity on Wednesday?
qa.a: The teacher sent him out on an errand so he wasn't watched, then asked privately what had been happening since Monday.

qa.q: What was the week like for Usha?
qa.a: Usha won the vote but faced Nilesh's scorn, and by Friday could work with him and share a win.

grounding: Shows a child's curled lip at a rival and trembling lip in front of classmates, and an adult protecting dignity and asking what happened before.

subtype: Curling a lip and lip trembling in embarrassment [Mismatch]
passage: Chetan, come, sit. Your Payal Bua has a story for you about lips. When I was ten, I was the queen in our school play, and in the middle of my big speech my mind went white. Silence. Someone in the front row giggled. I felt my lip start to shake, and I knew if I opened my mouth I'd cry in front of the whole school. Then Mrs D'Souza stepped out from the wings in her ordinary sari, holding a scroll. “Your Majesty, your letter,” she said, loud and grand. Inside was my line. Afterwards she asked only, “Did something upset you before the show?” I told her about my cousin's teasing, and she spoke to him that same day.

qa.q: What part did Payal play in the school play?
qa.a: Payal played the queen.

qa.q: What was young Payal feeling when her lip started to shake?
qa.a: She felt panicked and ashamed, afraid she would cry in front of the whole school after her mind went white.

qa.q: What choice did Mrs D'Souza make, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She stepped on stage as part of the play with the line on a scroll, rescuing Payal without showing her up, and later looked into the teasing before the show.

qa.q: How might the giggling child in the front row have seen the moment?
qa.a: They might have found the silence funny without realising Payal was close to tears.

grounding: Shows a child's trembling lip while holding back tears in front of others, and an adult protecting her dignity and asking what came before.

subtype: Curling a lip and lip trembling in embarrassment [Mismatch]
passage: Rain turned the school field to mud halfway through the final race. Dolma, in the lead, slipped at the bend and slid on her side. Ganga ran past and crossed first, then turned and curled her lip at Dolma, still in the mud. Dolma got up. Her lower lip was trembling hard, and the whole class was watching. The games teacher walked over, draped a towel round her like a cape and called to the crowd, “Everyone under the shed. Now.” Only then, alone, did the teacher kneel beside her. Later the teacher asked Ganga about the lip. Ganga's eyes flashed. “Last week she called me slowpoke in front of everyone.”

qa.q: Where did Dolma slip?
qa.a: Dolma slipped at the bend.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when her lower lip trembled?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and close to tears, having fallen in the mud while leading, with the whole class watching.

qa.q: How did the teacher protect Dolma's dignity in the rain?
qa.a: The teacher wrapped her in a towel and sent the crowd under the shed before kneeling to talk with her alone.

qa.q: What was behind Ganga's curled lip?
qa.a: Ganga was still angry and hurt about being called slowpoke last week, so the scorn had a history the teacher needed to hear.

grounding: Shows a child's lip curled in scorn at a rival and another's trembling lip in front of classmates, with an adult protecting dignity and asking what came before.

passage: Friday night. Diary of Bhupen. Papa came home late and sat at dinner with his lips pressed into a thin line. Ma said, “Pankaj, eat something,” but he only nodded. I was sure it was about my report card, which is on the fridge with a C in science. I ate my whole plate without talking. When I put my plate in the sink, I asked quietly, “Papa, are you angry with me?” He looked up, surprised. “With you? No, beta. The bus broke down and I stood for two hours. I'm just very tired.” Then he looked at the fridge. “Science on Sunday. Not angry. Tired.” I slept better than I thought.

qa.q: What grade was on the report card on the fridge?
qa.a: There was a C in science on the report card.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling while eating without talking?
qa.a: Bhupen felt anxious and guilty, sure that Papa's pressed lips meant anger about the science grade.

qa.q: What did asking quietly achieve?
qa.a: It showed Papa was tired from the broken-down bus, not angry, and it set a calm time to talk about science.

qa.q: How was the evening for Pankaj?
qa.a: Pankaj was exhausted from standing for two hours and was surprised that his tired face looked angry to his child.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's tightened lips as held-back anger, and a calm question showing it was tiredness.

passage: Nikita carried the lunch tiffin down the field path and found her Baba, Omkar, standing still by the broken fence, lips pressed so tight they'd gone white. Nikita slowed. Last time he looked like that, he shouted at everyone for an hour. She set the tiffin on the bund and waited. Then she asked, “Baba, are you angry?” He let out a long breath. “Yes. Not at you. Someone's goats got in and trampled the new onion rows.” His lips loosened a little. “Help me put up thorn branches after lunch?” Nikita nodded and handed him the first roti.

qa.q: What did the goats trample?
qa.a: The goats trampled the new onion rows.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she saw Baba's white, pressed lips?
qa.a: She felt nervous and wary, remembering the last time he looked like that and shouted for an hour.

qa.q: Why was waiting and then asking a good choice?
qa.a: It gave Omkar a moment to cool and a calm opening, so he could say he was angry but not at her, and ask for help.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Omkar?
qa.a: Omkar was angry about the trampled onions and holding it in, and felt some relief once he could say it aloud.

grounding: Shows a child correctly sensing restrained anger in a parent's tight lips, and a calm question showing it was not about her.

passage: In their kitchen in Stockholm, Lucia came in holding the vase she had just chipped. Her mother, Ingrid, sat at the table with a pile of forms, lips pressed flat, pen tapping. Lucia's heart sank. Mamma already looks furious, and she doesn't even know yet. Lucia nearly hid the vase behind her back. Instead she asked, “Are you cross?” Ingrid blinked up. “Cross? No, sweetheart. These school forms are just confusing, and I've been up since five.” Then she saw the vase. Her lips pressed again, for a second. “Ah. Tell me what happened.” Lucia did. It was only a small chip.

qa.q: What had Lucia chipped?
qa.a: Lucia had chipped the vase.

qa.q: What was Lucia feeling when she saw her mother's pressed lips?
qa.a: She felt scared and guilty, thinking Mamma was already furious before hearing about the chipped vase.

qa.q: What did asking “Are you cross?” make possible?
qa.a: It showed the tight lips came from confusing forms and tiredness, so Lucia felt safe enough to tell the truth about the vase.

qa.q: How did the morning feel for Ingrid?
qa.a: Ingrid was tired and focused on confusing forms, and her pressed lips were about concentration, not about Lucia.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's tightened lips as anger, and a calm question revealing tiredness and concentration instead.

passage: “Chaitanya, your turn for the deep end.” “No.” Chaitanya's jaw pushed forward, chin up, arms folded. “Everyone else has jumped.” “I said no.” Coach Zainab felt the other kids watching, waiting to see who would win. Zainab walked over and sat on the edge beside him, feet in the water. “Okay. Not jumping. Can you tell me what the no is about?” His jaw stayed out, but his voice cracked. “Last time water went up my nose and I couldn't breathe.” “That sounds really scary.” “It was.” “What if you sit and slide in, holding my hand, and I stay right there?” A long pause. “…Only holding.”

qa.q: What happened to Chaitanya last time?
qa.a: Last time water went up his nose and he couldn't breathe.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling behind his jutting jaw?
qa.a: He was frightened after water went up his nose last time; the defiant-looking jaw covered that fear, as his cracking voice shows.

qa.q: Why did sitting beside him work better than insisting?
qa.a: It stopped a contest in front of the others and let Chaitanya explain his fear, so Coach Zainab could offer a safer way in.

qa.q: What was the moment like for Coach Zainab with the other kids watching?
qa.a: Zainab felt pressure to win the standoff in front of the class, which made choosing to listen first harder.

grounding: Shows an adult reading a child's jutting jaw as defiance, then listening first and finding fear underneath.

passage: I'm Arohi. Last Diwali, Mumma told me to say sorry to my cousin Omkar for pushing him. I stuck my jaw out so far my teeth showed, and I said, “I won't.” Everyone called me stubborn. Mumma's voice got louder, and my jaw went further out. What nobody asked was why. Omkar had stamped on my clay diya, the one I'd painted for three days. I wasn't trying to be bad; I just wanted someone to hear that first. Later, Nani took me up to the terrace and asked. I told her, and cried. Then I said sorry to Omkar, and he said sorry about my diya.

qa.q: How long had Arohi spent painting the clay diya?
qa.a: Arohi had painted the diya for three days.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling while jutting the jaw out?
qa.a: Arohi felt hurt and unheard about the stamped-on diya, so the jaw showed a wish to be heard more than plain stubbornness.

qa.q: What did Nani do that the others didn't?
qa.a: Nani took Arohi aside and asked why, which let the hurt come out and made the apology possible.

qa.q: How did Mumma likely see the jutting jaw?
qa.a: Mumma likely saw defiance and got louder, not knowing about the stamped-on diya behind it.

grounding: Shows a child's jutting jaw read as defiance when it carried a wish to be heard, and listening first ending the standoff.

passage: Coach's note, Monday. Harish, PE. Nitin refused to go into the changing room before football today. He stood in the doorway with his jaw pushed out, fists at his sides, and said, “I'm not going in.” My first instinct was to give him a warning for defiance. I didn't. I told the rest to start warming up and asked Nitin to walk the boundary with me. After a lap he said the older boys have been flicking wet towels at him in there and laughing. His jaw was shaking by then. I changed the changing times from today and reported it to the head of year before lunch. The head of year spoke to the older boys this afternoon and phoned Nitin's parents.

qa.q: What had the older boys been doing in the changing room?
qa.a: The older boys had been flicking wet towels at Nitin in there and laughing.

qa.q: What does Nitin's shaking jaw suggest by the end of the walk?
qa.a: It suggests he was frightened and upset, and that the earlier jutting jaw was fear and a wish to be heard, not simple defiance.

qa.q: Which of Harish's choices mattered most?
qa.a: Holding back the warning and walking with Nitin away from the others let him speak; then Harish acted the same day by changing times and reporting it.

qa.q: What would change if Harish had given the warning?
qa.a: Nitin might have been punished while the towel-flicking went on, and he would learn that adults don't listen.

grounding: Shows an adult tempted to read a child's jutting jaw as defiance, listening first and finding fear, then acting the same day.
